concepts.def: An organ system in which several organs work together to digest and absorb food.
A large protein molecule that acts as a biological catalyst, speeding up a reaction in a living organism without being changed by it.
The part of an enzyme molecule that the substrate fits into. Its shape means the enzyme catalyses only one specific reaction.
A simplified model of enzyme action in which the substrate (the key) fits into the active site of the enzyme (the lock).
The change in the shape of an enzyme's active site caused by a high temperature or the wrong pH, so that the substrate no longer fits and the reaction stops.
The sum of all the reactions in a cell or in the body. These reactions are catalysed by enzymes.
The breakdown of food by digestive enzymes into small soluble molecules that can be absorbed into the bloodstream.
A carbohydrase is an enzyme that breaks down carbohydrates to simple sugars. Amylase is a carbohydrase which breaks down starch.
An enzyme that breaks down proteins to amino acids.
An enzyme that breaks down lipids (fats) to glycerol and fatty acids.

concepts.term: Sites of production of digestive enzymes
concepts.def: Amylase is produced in the salivary glands, the pancreas and the small intestine. Protease is produced in the stomach, the pancreas and the small intestine. Lipase is produced in the pancreas and the small intestine.
The small soluble molecules produced by digestion. They are used to build new carbohydrates, lipids and proteins, and some glucose is used in respiration.

An alkaline liquid made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder. It neutralises hydrochloric acid from the stomach and emulsifies fat to form small droplets, which increases the surface area. The alkaline conditions and large surface area increase the rate of fat breakdown by lipase.
An organ that pumps blood around the body. The right ventricle pumps blood to the lungs, where gas exchange takes place, and the left ventricle pumps blood around the rest of the body.
A circulation in which the blood passes through the heart twice for each complete circuit of the body: once on the way to the lungs and once on the way to the rest of the body.

concepts.term: Blood vessels associated with the heart
concepts.def: The vena cava carries blood into the heart from the body and the pulmonary artery carries blood from the heart to the lungs. The pulmonary vein carries blood from the lungs back to the heart and the aorta carries blood from the heart to the body. The coronary arteries supply the heart muscle itself.
Air passes down the trachea, into the bronchi and then into the alveoli, which are surrounded by a capillary network.
The tiny air sacs of the lungs, adapted for gaseous exchange by a large surface area, thin walls and the capillary network that surrounds them.
A group of cells located in the right atrium that controls the natural resting heart rate. Artificial pacemakers are electrical devices used to correct irregularities in the heart rate.
A blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart. Its wall is thick, containing muscle and elastic fibres, so that it withstands the high pressure of the blood.
A blood vessel that carries blood back towards the heart. Its wall is thin and it contains valves, because the blood is at low pressure.
A very narrow blood vessel with a wall one cell thick, so that substances can pass quickly between the blood and the tissues.
A tissue consisting of plasma, in which the red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets are suspended.
The liquid part of the blood, which transports the blood cells and dissolved substances around the body.
A blood cell that carries oxygen. It contains haemoglobin, has no nucleus and is a biconcave disc, giving a large surface area for the uptake of oxygen.
A blood cell that defends the body against pathogens, for example by engulfing them or by producing antibodies.
A small fragment of cell suspended in the plasma that helps the blood to clot at a wound.

A disease in which layers of fatty material build up inside the coronary arteries, narrowing them. This reduces the flow of blood through the coronary arteries, resulting in a lack of oxygen for the heart muscle.
Stents are used to keep the coronary arteries open. Statins are widely used to reduce blood cholesterol levels, which slows down the rate of fatty material deposit.
A heart valve that does not open fully, or that develops a leak, so that less blood is pumped or blood flows the wrong way. Faulty heart valves can be replaced using biological or mechanical valves.

In the case of heart failure a donor heart, or heart and lungs, can be transplanted. Artificial hearts are occasionally used to keep patients alive whilst waiting for a heart transplant, or to allow the heart to rest as an aid to recovery.
The state of physical and mental well-being.
Communicable diseases can be passed from one person to another, while non-communicable diseases cannot. Both are major causes of ill health.

Different types of disease may interact, for example defects in the immune system make infectious disease more likely, viruses living in cells can trigger cancers, and severe physical ill health can lead to depression and other mental illness.
Something that is linked to an increased rate of a disease. Risk factors can be aspects of a person's lifestyle, or substances in the person's body or environment.

An explanation of how a risk factor brings about a disease. A causal mechanism has been proven for some risk factors, but not in others, and many diseases are caused by the interaction of a number of factors.
Choosing a sample that is large enough and representative of the whole population, so that conclusions drawn from scientific data, including epidemiological data, are reliable.
The result of changes in cells that lead to uncontrolled growth and division.

Benign tumours are growths of abnormal cells which are contained in one area, usually within a membrane, and do not invade other parts of the body. Malignant tumour cells are cancers: they invade neighbouring tissues and spread to different parts of the body in the blood, where they form secondary tumours.
Lifestyle risk factors have been identified for various types of cancer, and there are also genetic risk factors for some cancers.

Knowledge of the digestive system from Key Stage 3 science is assumed: food passes through the mouth, stomach and small intestine, where it is broken down, and the small soluble products are absorbed in the small intestine.

A reaction written using the names of the substances rather than formulae, for example starch to sugars, or lipids to glycerol and fatty acids. Simple word equations should be understood; no chemical symbol equations are required.

mcqs.q: Enzymes catalyse specific reactions. What causes this specificity?
options: The temperature at which the enzyme works.
The shape of the enzyme's active site.
The amount of the enzyme that is used.
The pH at which the enzyme is stored.
mcqs.explain: Enzymes catalyse specific reactions in living organisms due to the shape of their active site, which only one substrate fits.

mcqs.q: Which statement describes the lock and key theory of enzyme action?
options: The enzyme fits into every kind of substrate.
The enzyme is used up by its own substrate.
The enzyme changes shape to fit any substrate.
The substrate fits the enzyme's active site.
mcqs.explain: In the lock and key theory, used as a simplified model of enzyme action, the substrate is the key that fits the active site of the enzyme.

mcqs.q: An enzyme-controlled reaction is fastest at 40 degrees Celsius. What happens at 60 degrees Celsius?
options: The rate falls because the enzyme has been killed.
The rate falls because the enzyme is used up.
The rate rises because the enzyme works faster.
The rate falls because the active site changes shape.
mcqs.explain: Above the optimum temperature the shape of the active site changes, so the substrate no longer fits and the rate falls.

mcqs.q: Protease in the stomach works fastest at pH 2. What happens to its activity at pH 8?
options: It falls, as the active site changes shape.
It rises, as enzymes work best at about pH 7.
It falls, as the enzyme is killed by alkali.
It falls, as the enzyme has been used up.
mcqs.explain: Away from its optimum pH the shape of the active site changes, so the substrate no longer fits and activity falls.

mcqs.q: Amylase broke down 20 mg of starch in 5 minutes. What was the mean rate of reaction?
options: 4 mg per minute
0.25 mg per minute
20 mg per minute
100 mg per minute
mcqs.explain: The mean rate is the amount changed divided by the time taken: 20 mg divided by 5 minutes.

mcqs.q: Enzymes are involved in metabolism. Which statement is correct?
options: Enzymes catalyse the reactions of metabolism in cells.
Enzymes give the reactions the energy that they need.
Enzymes are used up in the reactions that they speed up.
Enzymes catalyse only reactions that break down food.
mcqs.explain: Metabolism is the sum of all the reactions in a cell or the body, and each of those reactions is catalysed by an enzyme.

mcqs.q: Which statement about digestive enzymes is correct?
options: Bile is the enzyme that breaks down fat droplets.
One enzyme is able to digest every type of food.
Protease is made in the stomach and pancreas.
Amylase is made only in the wall of the stomach.
mcqs.explain: Protease is produced in the stomach, the pancreas and the small intestine, and it breaks down proteins to amino acids.

mcqs.q: What does lipase break lipids down into?
options: Glucose and fatty acids
Glycerol and fatty acids
Amino acids and simple sugars
Small droplets of lipid
mcqs.explain: Lipases break down lipids (fats) to glycerol and fatty acids, which are small soluble molecules that can be absorbed.

mcqs.q: Why does bile increase the rate of fat breakdown by lipase?
options: It digests the fat into fatty acids and glycerol.
It gives the lipase the energy that it needs.
It emulsifies fat, so surface area increases.
It makes the small intestine neutral at pH 7.
mcqs.explain: Bile emulsifies fat to form small droplets which increases the surface area, and the alkaline conditions and large surface area increase the rate of breakdown by lipase.

mcqs.q: What happens to the products of digestion after they are absorbed?
options: Every product is turned into glucose and stored.
They are all used in respiration to give energy.
They build new carbohydrates, lipids and proteins.
They join back to form the first food molecules.
mcqs.explain: The products of digestion are used to build new carbohydrates, lipids and proteins, and some glucose is used in respiration.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the double circulatory system is correct?
options: Blood passes through the heart once each circuit.
Arteries carry blood with oxygen to the lungs.
The right ventricle pumps blood to the lungs.
The left ventricle pumps blood to the lungs.
mcqs.explain: The right ventricle pumps blood to the lungs where gas exchange takes place, while the left ventricle pumps blood around the rest of the body.

mcqs.q: Which feature of the alveoli increases the rate of gaseous exchange?
options: A wide tube that carries air down to the lungs.
A thick outer wall that resists air pressure.
A supply of plasma that takes up the oxygen.
A large surface area and a good blood supply.
mcqs.explain: The alveoli are adapted for gaseous exchange by a large surface area and the capillary network that surrounds them.

mcqs.q: Which pairing of a blood vessel with its structure is correct?
options: Artery: thick wall resists the high pressure.
Vein: thick muscular wall resists high pressure.
Capillary: thick wall resists the blood pressure.
Artery: valves stop blood flowing backwards.
mcqs.explain: An artery carries blood away from the heart at high pressure, so its wall is thick, with muscle and elastic fibres.

mcqs.q: A heart pumps 300 cm3 of blood in 4 seconds. What is the rate of blood flow?
options: 1200 cm3 per second
75 cm3 per second
300 cm3 per second
0.01 cm3 per second
mcqs.explain: Rate of blood flow is the volume divided by the time taken: 300 cm3 divided by 4 seconds.

mcqs.q: A photograph shows the cells in a sample of blood. Which statement is correct?
options: Platelets move around the blood and destroy pathogens.
Plasma is the liquid that carries oxygen to the cells.
Red blood cells have a nucleus that controls oxygen use.
Red blood cells have no nucleus, so they carry more oxygen.
mcqs.explain: A red blood cell is adapted to its function of carrying oxygen: it has no nucleus, leaving more room for haemoglobin.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the treatment of coronary heart disease is correct?
options: Statins are used to widen the blocked coronary arteries.
Stents are used to keep the coronary arteries open.
Stents are used to lower the level of blood cholesterol.
Artificial hearts are used to cure the heart disease.
mcqs.explain: In coronary heart disease fatty material narrows the coronary arteries, and stents are used to keep them open.

mcqs.q: A person has a heart valve that has developed a leak. Which statement is correct?
options: Blood flows backwards through the leaking valve.
The volume of blood pumped stays the same.
Only a heart transplant can treat the problem.
An artificial heart gives a permanent cure.
mcqs.explain: A faulty valve that leaks lets blood flow backwards, so less blood is pumped forward to the body.

mcqs.q: Why might an artificial heart be used for a patient with heart failure?
options: It keeps a patient alive while awaiting a donor.
It replaces a faulty valve inside the patient.
It cures the heart failure without any further care.
It lowers the level of cholesterol in the blood.
mcqs.explain: Artificial hearts are occasionally used to keep patients alive whilst waiting for a heart transplant, or to allow the heart to rest as an aid to recovery.

mcqs.q: Which statement best describes health?
options: The state of being free of catching diseases.
The state of having no risk factors present.
The state of both physical and mental well-being.
The state of the body when disease is absent.
mcqs.explain: Health is the state of physical and mental well-being, so it is more than the absence of disease.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the interaction of different types of disease is correct?
options: Communicable disease has no effect on other illness.
Mental illness is not affected by physical illness.
Cancers are triggered by lifestyle, not by viruses.
An immune reaction to a pathogen can trigger allergies.
mcqs.explain: Different types of disease may interact: immune reactions initially caused by a pathogen can trigger allergies such as skin rashes and asthma.

mcqs.q: A scatter diagram shows a correlation between hours of exercise and heart health. What can be concluded?
options: Exercise has been proved to cause good heart health.
People who exercise avoid getting heart disease.
The variables are linked, but no cause is proven.
The sample size does not matter for this result.
mcqs.explain: A scatter diagram can be used to identify a correlation between two variables, but a causal mechanism has been proven for some risk factors and not for others.

mcqs.q: A scientist studies whether a substance is a risk factor using data from 20 people. Why is this a problem?
options: A risk factor affects each person in the sample.
The sample size has no effect on the result.
A correlation in the data would prove a cause.
The sample is too small to be representative.
mcqs.explain: The principles of sampling applied to epidemiological data require a sample large enough to represent the population before conclusions are drawn.

mcqs.q: Smoking is described as a risk factor for lung cancer. Which statement is correct?
options: A correlation in data proves that it is a cause.
It is a factor linked to an increased rate of disease.
It is the one risk factor for this type of cancer.
It leads to the disease in each person who smokes.
mcqs.explain: Risk factors are linked to an increased rate of a disease, and smoking is a lifestyle risk factor for lung disease and lung cancer.

mcqs.q: What is happening to the cells in a tumour?
options: Changes in cells lead to uncontrolled growth.
The cells in the tissue die and are not replaced.
Benign cells travel around in the bloodstream.
Lifestyle damages the membrane around the cell.
mcqs.explain: Cancer is the result of changes in cells that lead to uncontrolled growth and division.

mcqs.q: How do malignant tumour cells differ from benign tumour cells?
options: They stay inside a membrane in one part of the body.
They invade tissues and form secondary tumours.
They are caused by lifestyle rather than by genes.
They divide more slowly than normal healthy cells.
mcqs.explain: Malignant tumour cells are cancers: they invade neighbouring tissues and spread in the blood to different parts of the body, where they form secondary tumours.
